item.title: Mounting Instability in Pakistan: Consequences for Regional Security
Reignited violence in Ethiopia threatens to engulf the entire region
item.description:
Ethiopia is on the brink of another civil war.

Last week, fighting between rebels and federal forces in the northern Tigray, Amhara, and Afar states left hundreds dead. These clashes may signal the start of a potentially devastating conflict in a country still recovering from a bloody civil war that killed approximately 600,000 people between 2020 and 2022.

Fighting began as seven rebel groups from across various parts of the country announced the formation of a military coalition called the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival. The alliance’s expressed aim is to remove the federal government headed by Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed Ali from power.

Major fighting has thus far remained confined to the northern Tigray state, where the previous civil war took place. The leading rebel group, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), made significant territorial gains across the state last week, seizing control of Alula Aba Nega International Airport in the Tigrayan capital of Mekelle, as well as airports in the nearby cities of Axum and Shire. In response, Ethiopian Airlines shut down all service to those airports, cutting off much of Tigray to commercial air transit.

Following advances by rebel forces in Tigray, the Ethiopian military seems to have regained some territory in recent days. On Monday, the Ethiopian government and allied militias announced they had recaptured the strategic town of Alamata, about 75 miles south of Tigray’s capital.

Among those joining forces with the TPLF in this expansive rebellion is the Fano National Movement, a separatist coalition based in the country’s northern Amhara state that sided with the federal government against the TPLF in the last war. Once rivals, the TPLF and the Fano have now made common cause against the Ethiopian government.

In recent years, the Fano has been actively pursuing its own effort to end the “oppression” of the Amhara region from the country’s federal government and has clashed in armed conflict with federal forces in pursuit of that end. This new alliance thus accords with the Fano’s aim of securing greater independence from what it views as an overbearing federal government.

The recent uptick in violence follows months of growing tensions in Ethiopia. In May, the TPLF reclaimed control over the political administration of Tigray, arguing that the Ethiopian government had failed to follow through on its end of the Pretoria Agreement, which ended the previous civil war.

In the months since, sporadic fighting between federal forces and the TPLF has sprung up throughout Tigray. And the Ethiopian government’s drone warfare — which has killed civilians — has focused the attention of human rights activists, who argue such attacks should be investigated for possible war crimes.

Washington’s response to the renewed conflict has thus far mostly followed a wait-and-see approach, though growing violence in the country is beginning to attract attention on Capitol Hill. On Monday, Semafor reported that Senate Democrats, led by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), are pushing Secretary of State Marco Rubio to intervene in the conflict, though it remains unclear what such an intervention could look like.

The White House placed visa restrictions on unnamed TPLF officials in June following reports of clashes between the rebel group and federal forces. But just a couple weeks ago, Washington lifted sanctions on officials and the military of neighboring Eritrea — sanctions that the Biden administration had put in place during the previous war in an effort to curb Asmara’s role in that conflict. With these sanctions removed, Eritrea may find it easier to intervene in a renewed Ethiopian civil war.

In another case of twisting alliances, Eritrea was aligned with Ethiopia during the previous civil war, having viewed the TPLF and its aspirations as a threat to its own interests. But growing animosity between Ethiopia and Eritrea in the years since the Pretoria Agreement was signed has pushed the small coastal country to shift its support away from the federal government in Addis Ababa and toward the TPLF.

The root of the Eritrea-Ethiopia discord comes down to Ethiopia’s renewed determination to gain access to the Red Sea. Over the past couple years, Ethiopian officials have increasingly demanded free access to Eritrea’s Red Sea Port of Assab, which was under Ethiopian control until Eritrea’s independence from the country in 1993, at which time Ethiopia lost its coastline. Ethiopia has since signed an expensive agreement requiring it to pay between $1.5 and $2 billion annually in fees to neighboring Djibouti to use its Red Sea port, on which Addis Ababa relies for the vast majority of its maritime trade.

Another important player in the region’s complicated geopolitical chess match is Egypt, which has a long-running dispute with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD). The GERD, which was inaugurated on September 9, 2025 after about fourteen years of construction, is a massive dam upriver on the Nile that is the continent’s largest hydropower generator. Egyptian officials claim that the dam puts Egypt’s water security at risk, arguing that Ethiopia’s control of the dam will limit the amount of water that flows downstream, severely threatening Egypt’s vast irrigation system that sustains its agricultural economy.

As a result, Cairo has sought to gain leverage with Addis Ababa, in part by providing diplomatic support and, at times, military assistance to those of its neighbors with which it has strained relations or even overlapping territorial claims. They includeEritrea (via diplomatic support), Sudan (via diplomatic support and possible arms sales), and Somalia (via diplomatic support and troop deployments).

Sudan and Somalia themselves are in the throes of intense domestic conflicts. The Sudanese army is struggling in a brutal civil war against the Rapid Support Forces for control over the country. Meanwhile, Somalia continues its decades-long fight against armed groups while having to contend with the growing relations forming between foreign governments and multiple Somalian regions that claim independence from the central government.

This tangled web of alliances, mixed with intense domestic conflicts in surrounding countries, will make it difficult to contain a Tigrayan war. A multi-layered regional war has thus become a distinct possibility.

For now, the United States has little choice but to wait and see what happens, though targeted sanctions focused on entities that could fan the flames of war (such as Eritrean officials) should be considered on a case-by-case basis.

But any military intervention should be entirely off the table, particularly as the United States remains preoccupied with the mess caused by its ill-planned war against Iran.

item.title: Is Bibi cruising for a bruising by trolling Erdogan over Syria?
item.description:
During a speech at the United Nations last week, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu railed against Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, calling him a “tyrant.”

“Now he wants to take over Syria,” Netanyahu said. “Well, that's not surprising because he calls for Israel's destruction almost every single day.”

The comments come amid growing tensions between Israel and Turkey. In August, Israeli warplanes struck the Abu al-Duhur Airbase in northwestern Syria, roughly 43 miles from the Turkish border. The strike left craters in the runway and, as with earlier attacks around T4 and Palmyra in the Homs province, was carried out without prior notice to Ankara.

As Israeli aircraft approached the Turkish border, they were tracked by Turkish radar, bringing months of political and diplomatic tension between the two countries a step closer to direct military confrontation.

The Netanyahu government presents these strikes as preventive, aimed at stopping a larger Turkish encroachment into Syria before it starts. Israel’s concern is Turkey, which, alongside the United States, has become one of the main military and political partners of Syria's post-Assad government.

But Abu al-Duhur points to the opposite risk. In the absence of an immediate military threat, strikes aimed at preventing a potential future Turkish deployment may do more to raise the risk of a future conflict than to reduce it.

An imminent threat?


The Israeli prime minister's office justified the Abu al-Duhur strike by claiming it had intelligence indicating the base would be turned into a Turkish military facility. Ankara and Damascus firmly denied the claim. U.S. envoy Tom Barrack, a frequent target of Israeli criticism, had dined with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani in Istanbul on the eve of the strike and later said U.S. intelligence found nothing to support it.

But even if Israel's claim is accurate, whether a possible deployment amounted to an "immediate threat" requiring military action is a separate question.

According to retired Maj. Gen. Ateş Mehmet İrez, a former chief of operations in the Turkish Air Force, the reported Turkish visit to the base would, in operational terms, be a reconnaissance or assessment mission and would not necessarily indicate a desire to deploy troops there.

Turning a site survey into an operational deployment would take months in war-damaged Syria, İrez said. A radar may be physically installed within days, but power supply, communications, calibration, command-and-control integration and the sustainable deployment of personnel would take much longer.

"The picture described in Israel's justification, namely a permanent radar and air-defense network capable of restricting Israel's freedom of movement in Syrian airspace, is a matter of months, and most likely more than a year, rather than weeks," İrez told RS.

The real time pressure for Israel, he argued, lay elsewhere.

"Once Turkish personnel are physically present at an airbase, any subsequent strike on that same facility carries the risk of hitting the troops of a NATO member," he said. "From that perspective, the closing window was political, not technical."

The choice of target also supports that assessment. A runway is one of the fastest parts of an airbase to repair. If the objective had been to prevent the capability from emerging at all, Israel could have waited for harder-to-replace equipment to arrive. According to İrez, striking the runway and storage areas was aimed less at eliminating a capability than at establishing a precedent.

A radar would matter even if Turkey never fired a shot. It would turn unrecorded Israeli transits into documented events, with time, altitude and route. "What radar changes," İrez said, "is not merely control but the risk of proof."

From conduct to intent


When Syria shot down a Turkish RF-4E reconnaissance aircraft in 2012, there was still a government in Damascus that, even if imperfectly, accepted responsibility and could be dealt with diplomatically. İrez, then the Turkish Air Force's head of operations, briefed the cabinet during that crisis. Today, he said, Israeli strikes since December 2024 have left Syrian airspace "effectively ownerless." Until recently, Israel even blocked night flights at Syrian airports.

Among the most dangerous aspects of the Abu al-Duhur strike, in his view, is that Israel is shifting the threshold for a crisis from actual conduct to intent.

"Classical deterrence responds to something the other side has done. Here, the response is to something that has not yet been done," he said. "By moving the crisis threshold to the level of intent, this logic also changes the basis of the rules of engagement. Rules of engagement are tied to observable behavior or a violation. A threshold based on intent leaves the two sides without a common standard."

Unannounced Israeli operations near Turkey's border are not new. In 2007, Israeli jets crossed into Turkish airspace and dropped fuel tanks on Turkish soil during a mission to strike a suspected nuclear site near Deir ez-Zor.

"The increase in precautions in the region actually began in 2007, despite the good relations at the time," İrez said. "Measures that began as temporary steps in those years have since been expanded and made permanent."

The most recent of those steps came after Israel's strikes on T4 last year, when Ankara and Tel Aviv held technical deconfliction talks in Azerbaijan. A channel that one side (Israel) can bypass without warning is hardly a mechanism at all.

Restraint, for now


Turkey’s 2015 shootdown of a Russian Su-24 is still the most widely remembered case of Ankara enforcing its rules of engagement along the Syrian border, but it was not the first.

After the RF-4E crisis, Ankara tightened those rules. Turkish F-16s then shot down a Syrian Mi-17 in 2013 and a MiG-23 in 2014 after airspace violations.

At Abu al-Duhur, Turkey chose restraint. Turkey, İrez said, “tracked the flights and took precautions, but refrained from intervening despite the aircraft passing close to the border.”

But Ankara's calculation is not purely military. In Turkey, the current tensions are widely attributed to Netanyahu's choices rather than to a permanent rift with Tel Aviv. Israel's election campaign, in which Likud has featured Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan on its billboards, is being followed in Ankara and across Turkish media almost as closely as a domestic one. Part of Turkey's restraint reflects a concern that responding would mean taking the bait and handing Netanyahu a crisis to campaign on. That concern is shared inside Israel. When Netanyahu posed in front of a fighter jet to warn of pre-election attacks, the opposition accused him of using military bases as campaign props.

Still, that does not mean Ankara's patience is unlimited. As İrez warned, "Operations in Syria based solely on anticipation are creating an atmosphere in which tensions can easily turn into a direct military confrontation."

Nor do such strikes solve the problem Israel says it faces. Air power may delay the alleged future deployment, but it cannot stop the growing integration between Turkey and Syria. Ankara's role in Syria goes well beyond a single airbase. Turkey is helping rebuild the Syrian state in areas ranging from its army to its power grid.

Syrian units train at Turkish army facilities, Syrian cadets study at Turkish military academies, and Syrian troops joined EFES, Turkey's flagship exercise, for the first time this year. Ankara has supplied armored vehicles, trains Syrian police, and its intelligence service works closely with Damascus. Just 12 days after the Abu al-Duhur strike, and despite Israel's warnings against Turkish moves toward the south, Turkish and Syrian forces completed their second joint floating bridge over the Euphrates in Deir ez-Zor.

The rivalry between Turkey and Israel is unlikely to end in the near term. Keeping it from turning into a kinetic conflict in Syria, however, is achievable. Having chosen to give the new government in Damascus a chance, Washington now carries a continuing responsibility to help stabilize Syria and to keep two close allies out of an avoidable conflict.

The U.S. has already said it is working on a trilateral deconfliction mechanism. The task now is to turn it into a direct political channel with clear rules on notification, so that future incidents can be managed before they spark a military confrontation.

item.title: They aren't uniformed, but these US companies are fighting for Ukraine
item.description:
This summer, Microsoft announced that “it will extend its provision of technology support to Ukraine through the end of 2027,” providing technology, cybersecurity support, and other assistance to help Ukraine maintain essential digital services during the war.”

Not only U.S. weapons, but a host of U.S. tech companies have gone to war in Ukraine. This includes PayPal, now one of the biggest multinational online payment systems in the world, which got into the act, cutting off access to all Russian accounts when Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022.

Palantir initially offered its services to Ukraine for free. Meanwhile is has used the Ukraine War as a proving ground for its emerging technology, has worked with Ukraine to develop AI to sift and analyze battlefield intelligence and plan and coordinate deep strike operations. This now extends to controlling drone swarms and identifying targets. It now has partnerships across numerous Ukraine ministries, including a huge deal announced in May to broaden the use of AI across all military and civilian defense operations. In 2022 Palantir’s market capitalization was less than $25 billion, today it is closer to $450 billion.

Meanwhile, Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite systems make it possible for the Ukrainian armed forces to communicate, track the movement of Russian troops, and select targets. In his book The Russo-Ukrainian War: Follies of Empire, Richard Sakwa says the provision of that ability “was crucial for Ukraine’s early success in defeating the Russian advance on Kiev.”

While Musk has been opposed to the Ukrainian military using Starlink for deep strikes into Russia — a position he affirmed in August — Ukraine’s use of Starlink for mid-strike drones has clearly transformed the war in Ukraine. Jennifer Kavanagh, Senior Fellow & Director of Military Analysis at Defense Priorities, told RS that “Ukraine would not be able to carry out its current military campaign without Starlink's support.”

Last year, Musk claimed that the Ukrainian military’s “entire front line would collapse if I turned it off.”

Providing free satellite service to Ukraine became expensive for Musk. A year and a half into the war, Musk threatened to terminate his services unless the U.S. government picked up the tab. So, they did. The Polish government has also said that it pays for Starlink services in Ukraine, contributing $50 million a year.

Microsoft’s mobilization for Ukraine has been much quieter. Most of us thought the war began on February 24, 2022. According to Microsoft president Brad Smith, it started the day before. “That’s when we saw 300 Russian-coordinated cyberattacks all seek to down the Ukrainian government.” That’s also when, in the words of the New York Times, “Microsoft threw itself into the middle of a ground war in Europe.”

As the story goes, “wiper” malware attempted to wipe clean the data of hundreds of server systems belonging to the Ukrainian government. Microsoft’s Threat Intelligence Centre was the first to see it, according to Henry Farrell and Abraham Newman in their book, Underground Empire: How America Weaponized the World Economy. Separated by an ocean, Microsoft personnel “were manning Ukraine’s front lines.” They quickly shared their intel with Ukraine’s cyberdefense officials, and, within hours, Ukraine’s virus detections systems had been updated and the attacking code had been blocked.

Microsoft, Farrell and Newman write, had forged “a closer relationship with the Ukrainian government and the national security advisors and team there.” They had become Ukraine’s “shield… against waves of attacks.”

As if its own nation, Microsoft announced that they “condemn this unjustified, unprovoked and unlawful invasion by Russia,” and immediately “suspend[ed] all new sales of Microsoft products and services in Russia.”

In 2022, the New York Times wrote how tech executives, including those from Microsoft, were granted security clearances and sat in on secure briefings by the NSA and U.S. Cyber Command. Microsoft and Google were the sources behind most of the shared actionable intelligence. At the time, Microsoft had established “24/7 sharing of threat intelligence” so that “work[ing] closely with Ukrainian government officials and cybersecurity staff” they could “identify and remediate threat activity against Ukrainian networks” and “defend against attacks.”

In a revealing interview four years ago, Microsoft president Brad Smith said what Microsoft has “done first is, frankly, to support and defend Ukraine.” Drawing a military analogy, Smith spoke like a cyberwar general, comparing the situation to a classic military maneuver: “you’ve got to disperse your defensive assets so they’re not vulnerable to a single attack.”

According to a June 2026 Microsoft report, the tech giant has spent more than $700 million providing Ukraine with technology and cybersecurity. If Microsoft were a country, that would rank it in the top 25 supporters of Ukraine.

The Russian-Ukrainian war has changed the nature of warfare. Rifles and tanks, The Wall Street Journal opines, are “going the way of sword fights and cavalry charges” now that “thumbs on joysticks have largely replaced fingers on triggers and more fighting is done on screens and less in trenches.”

Though Brad Smith says Microsoft is “a company and not a government or country,” he has “made it clear,” according to the New York Times, it “is not a neutral one.” Huge tech companies, like Microsoft, SpaceX and Palantir, like countries, have chosen sides and allied with the U.S. and Ukraine, partnering with them as essential players on a transformed battlefield. The technology these companies have sent to Ukraine has been as important as the weapons that allied countries have sent.

“Your ability to identify the right technology and implement it will determine what happens on the battlefield,” Palantir CEO Alex Karp said in 2023, adding that Palantir is “responsible for most of the targeting in Ukraine.” In the same year he said he’s “in favor of a robust posture in America” and that Palantir wants people who want to be on the side of the West, making the West a better society, more able to defend themselves.”

When Russia invaded Ukraine, the U.S. and its partner countries sent weapons. Tech giants like Microsoft, SpaceX, and Palantir sent technology, expressed their ideological loyalty to Ukraine, and joined its side in the war. Many might think that behavior is natural, especially when the cause is considered a righteous one back home.

Others may believe it crosses a line, that it helps prolong a destructive war that won’t ultimately be won on the battlefield, while bolstering profits for shareholders and salaries for company executives.

Somehow, that doesn’t feel right.

item.description:
The risks of AI aren’t what we think they are, as a recent security incident between China and the United States reveals

Amid a barrage of news stories warning about superintelligent machines rendering humanity extinct, a CNN story describing the opposite scenario – one in which the US military’s reliance on brittle chatbots almost brought the US into war with China – went mostly unnoticed by the public.

The biggest international AI news of the past three weeks was Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon’s resignation. According to him, OpenAI and Anthropic are “racing straight towards self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives”. Coxon’s description of a “terminator” scenario, a machine becoming much smarter than humanity and deciding to wipe us out, captured the public, journalists’ and politicians’ attention, stirring waves of fear-inducing, credulous reporting, and policy actions.

Timnit Gebru is executive director of Dair and author of the forthcoming book Deep Unlearning: The Radicalization of a Tech Idealist, which is available for preorders now and set to publish on 16 February.

item.title: War, power games and impunity. I watched the farce that is the UN general assembly: what a tragedy, what a mess | Nesrine Malik
item.description:
Ukraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan: it has so many problems to confront and fails to do so. Seen up close, it is a study in stasis and decline

UN general assembly meetings are not usually riveting occasions. But this year’s encapsulated a world in flux and crisis, an international law and organisation structure that is falling apart, and a humanitarian order machine running hot. What unfolded was less a gathering for resolution and resolve than a display of showboating, frustration and fractiousness.

It was a snapshot for the history books of four huge destabilising conflicts for which there seems to be no means of, or interest in, resolution – Ukraine, Iran, Palestine and Sudan. Volodymyr Zelenskyy delivered an account of five years of Russian aggression: the staggering loss of life – hundreds of thousands killed on both sides – the porousness of the sanctions on Russia, the “madness” of it all. Donald Trump once again threatened to “annihilate” Iran if it did not make a deal, a promise that has now been made so many times its restating only reveals its hollowness. Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, responded in his own speech by saying that Iran has been the victim of US terrorism and aggression, and would defend itself with the “utmost strength”. The sole US delegation representative in the room walked out.

Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

Two years after Israel killed Hassan Nasrallah, Hezbollah is weaker but not finished. WaTaawanou, a crowdfunded charity outside Hezbollah’s formal hierarchy, exemplifies one way Hezbollah endures: outsourcing part of the cost of sustaining – and retaining – its Shiite base. Israel eliminated its seniormost military and political leadership, over 5,000 fighters, and significant parts of its arsenal, while its finances are strained. Even as Tehran reportedly moved more than $1 billion to the group after the November 2024 ceasefire – and another $1 billion the following year – Bashar al-Assad’s fall has severely constricted Hezbollah’s transfer routes from Iran through Syria. Yet Hezbollah can survive and regenerate if it preserves the Shiite constituency supplying its manpower and, more importantly, domestic political protection.

WaTaawanou began as an informal relief campaign in November 2019. Founder Afif Shouman identifies it with Hezbollah’s “Resistance environment,” though in an October 2022 interview he said it “does not belong to Hezbollah.” Because WaTaawanou is not U.S.-sanctioned, it can solicit funds through channels Hezbollah’s designated institutions cannot use as freely, including Whish Money, OMT/Western Union, MoneyGram, and direct contributions. It also has an account at Hezbollah’s sanctioned quasi-bank, Al-Qard al-Hassan. Its public-relations director says most Lebanese donors give $5 or $10, but together fund larger campaigns. Whish closed WaTaawanou’s account in October 2025, but its websitestill lists Whish and bank transfers via an International Bank Account Number (IBAN), without usable details for either. Larger projects have drawn support from Lebanese private donors, expatriates, Iranian-linked organizations, and Iraq’s al-Sawaed tribal network.

Yet WaTaawanou’s formal separation from Hezbollah belies extensive ties. Shouman says Hezbollah was the only outside organization to embrace and assist it and credits its development to Nasrallah’s “direct and foundational guidance.” He says former Hezbollah Executive Council chairman Hashem Safieddine treated WaTaawanou as “a principal file.” WaTaawanou has repeatedly worked with Hezbollah’s Social Action apparatus and Islamic Health Committee. At least two volunteers—Ali Lutfi Faran and Amine Hassan Badreddine—served as Hezbollah fighters. Shouman said its 2024 wartime relief proceeded in “full coordination with Hezbollah.”

That relationship is clearest in its spending. Its beneficiaries extend beyond Hezbollah supporters, but its aid eases material pressure across the overwhelmingly Shiite base on which Hezbollah depends. Shouman says it aided 94,000 families during the 2024 war with food, medicine, cash, and shelter. Since the November 27 ceasefire, its Al-Wajh al-Hassan reconstruction project has used donations in war-damaged, overwhelmingly Shiite southern municipalities including Ramyeh, Houla, and Mays al-Jabal, installing prefabricated housing and classrooms, repairing schools, aiding farmers, and distributing food. WaTaawanou also channels money to Hezbollah-linked entities, including payments to Al-Rasoul al-Aazam Hospital and Saint Georges Hospital–Hadath, both Martyrs Foundation hospitals. It also purchased fuel from Amana Fuel, which the foundation controls through Atlas Holding. Treasury designated the Martyrs Foundation in 2007 and calls its Lebanon office an integral element of Hezbollah’s support network. WaTaawanou paid Hezbollah’s Islamic Health Committee through Dar al-Hawraa Medical Center and repeatedly paid Al Moukhtar Products, which Treasury designated as part of a Hezbollah business network.

WaTaawanou therefore gives Hezbollah two benefits: outside donors cover costs Hezbollah would otherwise bear, while WaTaawanou channels the credit back to Hezbollah. Nasrallah portraits line its premises, his face brands Al-Wajh al-Hassan, and Hezbollah flags and insignia appear at its events. Shouman says its role complements Hezbollah’s: Hezbollah’s fighters defend the community while WaTaawanou supports the group’s Shiite base.

WaTaawanou cannot alone explain Hezbollah’s Shiite support, but efforts on this scale likely help preserve it. Studiesshow many Shiites are drawn to Hezbollah less by ideology than by the security, services, and communal advancement it provides, while regular patronage recipients are likelier to oppose the group’s disarmament, support its political role, and credit it for reconstruction. That constituency remains overwhelmingly behind Hezbollah. A late 2024 survey found 85 percent trusted Hezbollah. An estimated 700,000–900,000 people attended Nasrallah’s February 2025 funeral, and three months later Hezbollah and the AMAL Movement, Lebanon’s other major Shiite party, dominated municipal elections in heavily Shiite southern and eastern districts. Gallup found in June-July 2025 that 69 percent opposed giving the Lebanese Army exclusive control over weapons. In April-May 2026, Information International found 87.5 percent opposed Hezbollah’s disarmament.

For Beirut, forcibly disarming Hezbollah therefore risks confronting not simply an armed organization, but one still backed by most of what is probably Lebanon’s largest sect. Lebanon has held no official census since 1932, but independent pollster Statistics Lebanon estimates Shiites at 32.2 percent of citizens. Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem has rejected disarmament even when paired with Israeli withdrawal, and on June 17, 2026 declared that “any project to disarm us will not pass.”

Lebanon has consequently paired categorical disarmament decisions with reluctance to enforce them coercively. On March 2, the cabinet banned Hezbollah’s military and security activity and ordered it to surrender its weapons, but Prime Minister Nawaf Salam said Beirut did “not seek a confrontation with Hezbollah,” while President Joseph Aoun insisted the state monopoly over arms proceed through dialogue “away from force.” Five days later, army commander Rodolph Haykal said national unity and internal stability came first and “the solution is not solely a military one.” In September, official sources said its Nabatieh deployment was not intended to make the city weapons-free. South Litani Sector deputy commander Colonel Raja Amer told CNN the army would proceed “slowly” rather than use violence against “our own people,” agreeing that avoiding another civil war was central to its approach.

On September 9, the army claimed “operational control” in three test zones under the U.S.-brokered June 26 Israel-Lebanon Framework Agreement to clear unauthorized fighters, weapons, and military infrastructure. But it identified no Hezbollah fighter disarmed or arrested, and no Hezbollah depot, tunnel, or command center dismantled. WaTaawanou helps preserve the communal support that makes such coercion politically dangerous. For a battered Hezbollah, Beirut’s reluctance to test that support buys it the resource regeneration requires above all: time.

item.title: BLUF: Russian Strategic Culture Drives its Callous and Brutal Actions
item.description:
My friends and family often ask me why Russia behaves so offensively. They are baffled by Russia’s lack of humanity and Moscow’s actions such as hiring assassins, launching drones at innocents, and planning economic sabotage against international companies. While not an excuse, just an explanation, scholars of Russia understand the country’s deep sense of insecurity and vulnerability. Its longing to be a part of Europe, and its own view that its rightful place as a global leader are all driving Russia’s barbaric actions. According to strategic culture theorists, a state’s approach to war is shaped by its cultural and historical experiences, including geography, religion, language, and national identity. These factors influence a state’s perception of security threats, willingness to use military force, and approach to diplomacy and negotiation. They also help us to anticipate a state’s actions.

Russian strategic culture reflects a worldview shaped by centuries of conflict, invasion, brutality against others, inflicted on its people from foreign powers and by the government against its own population, and foiled attempts to become card carrying members of the west. Key elements of Russian strategic culture include the belief that the rest of the world, especially the West consistently undermines Russia and thwarts it rightful place as a world leader, and a belief in the necessity of military strength to push back the West. When the West does not push back, Moscow believes that their tactics are working.

Insecurity Drives Every Move

Russia’s persistent awareness of vulnerability and deep-seated mistrust of its neighbors is deeply ingrained and a consequence of centuries of historical experience. This insecurity manifests as a deep-seated suspicion of the West and a zealous determination to maintain control over Russia’s perceived sphere of influence. Understanding the historical currents that have shaped this perception is crucial for comprehending Russia’s present-day actions.

Russia’s experiences with wars and conflicts, such as the Mongol invasion, Napoleonic Wars, World War I, and World War II, have reinforced the idea that the country is constantly under threat and must be prepared to defend itself at all times. The Russian feeling of vulnerability and insecurity, particularly concerning interactions with “Western countries” is ingrained. To counter this insecurity Russian leaders have long highlighted the importance of having buffer zones on its borders. Removing those buffer zones heightens Russia’s sense of vulnerability.

From as early as the 18th century, Russian imperial strategy was heavily influenced by the need to create and maintain buffer zones along its western borders. Peter the Great and Catherine the Great both conquered lands on Russia’s borders so that Moscow would have a buffer from invasion. This proactive doctrine was aimed at insulating the Russian heartland from European powers. The annexation of Baltic territories, the absorption of Finland, and the partitioning of Poland were all manifestations of this strategy. These territorial acquisitions were driven by a pragmatic logic: to push potential adversaries further away and create a strategic depth that would absorb any initial blows in case of conflict. Russia continues to try to use buffer states or “allies” to keep others from its immediate vicinity, but this is an increasingly difficult task for Moscow as its former republics and satellite countries choose new alliances and partners.

Germany’s invasion of Russia in 1941 was a defining moment in Russia’s historical experience. This invasion resulted in some 27 million Soviet deaths and widespread devastation. It cemented Russia’s profound sense of betrayal from the West, and a visceral need for absolute security. World War II profoundly shaped Russia’s post-war security calculus, leading to a pursuit of military strength and a zero-tolerance policy for any perceived threat on its borders. The narrative of this war is deeply embedded in Russian society, serving as a constant reminder of the price of vulnerability and the imperative of never allowing such an event to recur. Putin’s family was directly affected by WW2 with his brother dying of starvation during the siege of Leningrad, his Grandmother killed by the Germans in Tver, and his father being severely injured during combat duties. He often discusses this in his speeches.

The post-Soviet era where East European nations and former Soviet Republics are joining NATO and the EU is particularly distressing for Moscow. The historically more neutral northern European countries joining NATO also is alarming to Moscow. From Moscow’s perspective, the loss of Ukraine to the West represents not just a geopolitical setback, but the obliteration of a crucial defensive buffer. We are also seeing Moscow’s anxiety rising regarding Armenia’s recent moves toward the West.

During the first summer of the Ukrainian war, Putin compared himself to Peter the Great and likened the invasion of Ukraine to the eighteenth century Russian Czar’s wars. This underscores the mindset of Russian leaders and shows that their history is never far from them.

Earning for Inclusion

Russia’s geographic position has greatly impacted its strategic culture. Russia is the biggest country in the world, and while only 23 percent of the country is in Europe, almost 80 percent of the population lives there. This makes Europe extremely important for Russia. One can see this link throughout Russian history. Even from the founding of the modern Russian state in the sixteenth century, its foreign interests were linked to Europe. When Peter the Great established an empire, the interconnections with Europe increased. Russia conducted wars and created alliances with different European countries. Russian nobles were stung when European nobles mocked them and called them uncouth and barbaric.

Today, the Kremlin emphasizes narratives that underscore Western hostility, and Russia’s role as a decisive power in European affairs. These narratives reinforce Russia’s claims to special rights in regional security and justify to itself and its people, assertive foreign policy actions, including military interventions in neighboring states. Any expansion of western power such as expansion of NATO and deployment of U.S. forces in Europe are perceived as existential threats to the Russian state and infringing on Russia’s rightful relationship with Europe, just as they were during the Soviet-era.

Demanding a Seat at the Table

For centuries, leaders of the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union emphasized Russia as a great power. During the Cold War, Russia, through the Soviet Union, was able to act as a global leader. After the collapse of the Soviet Union, Russian leaders were confronted with the fact that Russia had limited “spheres” of influence.

A main aim of Russian foreign policy under Putin is regaining and maintaining great power status. Putin repeats in his speeches that Russia is a great power and that the West, especially the United States, does not give Russia the respect it deserves. The Russian people support this view. Moscow remains angered that in its view, after the Cold War, the United States created a unipolar world and used NATO to maintain its hegemonic status. Putin has consistently publicly lamented the breakup of the USSR as “the greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the century.” More recently, Putin has said, “At last, Russia has returned to the world arena as a strong state - a country that others heed and that can stand up for itself.”

Russian leaders view Russia’s military might, both kinetic and grey zone activities, as their way to press for global leader status. They believe that Russia must take what it believes is its due such as Ukraine. Russian leaders also contend that it must make the West uncomfortable with continued attacks such as the drone incursions, assassinations, and ongoing disinformation. Pressing this avenue, in their view, wil make the West eventually give up on pushing back on Russia and allow Russia to take its rightful place as a global leader.

Implications for Policy and Security

None of this explanation of Russia’s national security mindset is meant to apologize for Russia’s barbaric behaviors. It is meant to help negotiators and policy maker understand Russia’s perspective, however misinformed and self-determined. Russian strategic culture emphasizes an assertive approach to conflict which is meant to make up for Russian feelings of vulnerability and being outcast from the West. This approach is evident in Russia’s actions in Ukraine, where strategic culture drives Russia’s actions.

Moscow’s lack of trust in the West is underscored by Putin and his circle who are the representatives of the “greatest generation” of the Soviet Union. These leaders grew when the state was a global power and controlled parts of Europe. They came to the pinnacle of their careers when the West, having forced the breakup of the Soviet Union, attempted to replace Soviet and Russian culture with Western values. They are bitter about this.

Having a realistic view of Russia’s perceived right and left limits allows negotiators and military planners to develop a workable way ahead in foreign relations. It should not limit US actions in calling out Russia’s morally and ethically abhorrent actions but it should inform our actions.

In summary, Russian strategic culture is driven by a sense of vulnerability, a focus on wanting to be part of the cool club of European nations, and an outsized view that Russia should be a global leader, regardless of its barbaric actions.

Russian and Ukrainian Clashing Strategic Cultures

Russia and Ukraine both see a negative outcome of the current war as an existential threat to their existence. That means that negotiating a settlement is difficult, herculean, and likely under the current circumstances an impossible task. Diplomacy alone cannot produce a durable settlement, because the two strategic cultures are incompatible. At most, military exhaustion could produce an armistice that freezes the conflict without resolving it. Before Russia’s insecurity can be addressed, the rest of the world must make it clear that Russia will maintain pariah status if it continues its slaughter of Ukrainian citizens and attacks in the west. The third-party sanctions recently passed by Congress are a step in the right direction. Sanctions alone, however, will not stop Russia whose people are used to hardship and even expect it. I am usually an optimist but for now, unfortunately, I cannot see a positive way forward in this war. The themes that Ukraine and Russia have woven through their strategic cultures indicate that there will be more deaths, destruction, and hardship before this war ends. The best that the world can do is to contain the violence and help Ukraine continue to strengthen its statehood while calling out each and every Russian atrocity.

item.title: War has returned to Tigray. This time it may not stay in Ethiopia
item.description:
War has returned to Tigray. This time it may not stay in Ethiopia Expert comment LToremark 1 October 2026

As fighting escalates in Tigray and neighbouring areas, there are fears that Ethiopia’s internal instability could spill over into the wider Horn of Africa region.

Conflict returned to Ethiopia’s northern region of Tigray on 23 September, as the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) forces stormed three national airports in Tigray. In what the TPLF claimed was defensive combat, ground offensives were also expanded along Tigray’s southern and eastern borders with the neighbouring Amhara and Afar regions. The TPLF and its allies captured parts of Afar but lost several key areas in southern Tigray, including Alamata town.

Ethiopia’s federal government forces and the allied Tigray Peace Force (TPF) are now advancing towards Mekelle, the capital of Tigray. Meanwhile, reports of drone strikes in Addis Ababa and on government-controlled airbases alters the nature of the war.

Although Tigray has seen conflict before, this time there is a risk that hostilities could extend into Eritrea and Sudan.

The slow creep towards renewed conflict

Related work

Ethiopia needs more than an election to calm internal and regional conflict

The risk of renewed hostilities in Tigray had been clear for some time, given the steady decline in relations between the federal government and the TPLF. The failure to build on the Pretoria Agreement – the ceasefire deal that brought an end to the war in 2022 – was largely the result of a continued zero-sum approach by both sides, as well as weak implementation and oversight.

The agreement effectively unravelled in May, when the TPLF reinstated a pre-war legislative council, with its chairman Debretsion Gebremichael named regional president. This spelled the end of the Tigray Interim Regional Administration (TIRA) – a key outcome negotiated under Pretoria. The removal of interim president, General Tadesse Werede, formerly head of the Tigray Defense Forces (TDF), followed the ouster of his predecessor Getachew Reda in late 2024.

The TPLF views the recent escalation as a return to full-scale war. To an extent, they have been pushed towards a response. There is continued containment of Tigray; a lack of implementation of the Pretoria Agreement or any dispute resolution mechanism; the absence of incentives for its leadership to return to the federal fold; a weakening of TPLF legitimacy in the region; and recent drone attacks by the government in the region.

But unlike in the 2020–22 war, the federal government has been more cautious and calculated in its actions as well as public messaging. The government frames the TPLF as a rogue administration that is colluding with internal opposition insurgencies and external actors to threaten Ethiopia’s territorial integrity and its own survival.

The key question now is whether the government will seek to contain the conflict within Tigray and other parts of northern Ethiopia, or whether it will consider it necessary to pursue bolder options. One such option could be targeting Eritrea, which it believes to be supporting anti-government movements – something Eritrea has repeatedly denied. In a message assigning culpability to its northern neighbour, Ethiopia closed its embassy in Eritrea and expelled Eritrean diplomats.

Now, much will depend on how the conflict evolves.

Internal division in Tigray and a new opposition alliance

The TPLF’s control over Tigrayan society has weakened significantly. Since the war ended in 2022, it has faced protests over crippling economic conditions, growing competition from rival parties and defections by leading members. In recent months, Tigrayan authorities have turned to forcibly recruiting young men into the defence forces and have cracked down on freedom of speech. For the people of Tigray, an already difficult humanitarian situation now looks set to worsen. 

There is deep division within TPLF too. Following the start of the military offensive, there have been reports of senior TPLF officials being arrested or defecting to Addis Ababa.

Days before the fighting resumed, the TPLF and six other regional armed opposition groups – including Amhara’s Fano movement and the Oromia region’s Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) – announced a coalition called the Alliance for Survival. Their common goal is to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and his Prosperity Party from power and install a transitional government.

But it is not immediately clear that this uneasy tactical alliance – among groups with unresolved tensions and very different visions for Ethiopia – will result in functional cooperation. Senior leaders of Fano have publicly opposed the alliance; while a recently divided OLA may struggle with justification to its support base. There are also historical grievances between some of these groups. The TPLF have accused Fano and the Eritrean forces of grave human rights violations in Tigray four years ago, while Fano and OLA have been bitter and at times violent enemies.

Risk of regional spillover

Related work

De-escalation is needed to prevent Ethiopia and Eritrea from going to war

Opposition to the Ethiopian government also comes from beyond the country’s borders. Tsimdo is a transnational alliance which reportedly links the TPLF, the Eritrean government and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF).

The TPLF is silently allied with its former foe, Eritrea, with supply lines chiefly secured through Tigray’s northern border. But the Eritrean government’s priority is to keep war away from its own territory, and its alleged support for opposition groups increases the risk of further regional escalation – especially with Ethiopia eyeing control over Eritrea’s Red Sea port of Assab.

Meanwhile, the conflicts in Ethiopia and Sudan have also become more intertwined. The Ethiopian government has accused the SAF of backing the TPLF – which they have denied – and is increasingly unsettled by the reported presence of Tigrayan fighters alongside the SAF in eastern Sudan. It fears that the SAF, in collaboration with Eritrea, could reinforce the TPLF from across the Sudanese border – including near strategic sites like the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam.

Sudan, in turn, has accused Ethiopia of providing support for the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudan People’s Liberation-North (SPLM-N), including training, supplies and use of Ethiopian territory. Ethiopia’s close ally, the UAE, is also accused of supporting the RSF – although it refutes such allegations. Ethiopia’s calculus is seemingly to create a buffer on its border with Sudan. However, direct dialogue and de-escalation with the SAF would go further than retaliatory exchanges and mutual accusations of interference.

Limited options for de-escalation  

The mediation landscape is very different from 2022. Members of the international community have called out the TPLF for their escalatory actions and urged a return to African Union (AU)-led talks. The Ethiopian government has so far controlled the narrative around this conflict, briefing foreign governments about the likely escalation ahead of the UN General Assembly.

The Pretoria Agreement did not produce the broader political settlement needed for durable peace and no longer seems tenable for either side. The TPLF has repeatedly discredited the only existing mediation effort under the AU. Hardening regional rivalries and the lack of US or wider Western interest to fully support the AU with the resources and leverage needed to create a viable platform, makes a sustainable resolution to this conflict seem a long way off.

Given these conditions, the conflict is likely to continue for a while. However, the danger of diplomatic inaction is that a protracted war in Tigray is likely to spill over beyond Ethiopia, into Eritrea and further into Sudan. Policymakers must find a way to take collective action to avert such a dangerous regional escalation.

Iran Calls Itself the Victim, Its Record Tells Another Story
item.description:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s speech at the United Nations did not mention Iran’s history of terrorism and the thousands of innocent victims killed, or the imprisonment and killing of thousands of its own people who were peacefully protesting, or the repeated enrichment of uranium at levels close to 90% purity for nuclear weapons or repeatedly denying access to International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors to suspect nuclear sites in Iran. There was no attempt by Mr. Pezeshkian to deny these allegations or justify Iran’s sick behavior, or to concede that Iran’s leadership will address these accusations and change its behavior. Rather, it was a recitation of how the U.S. leadership had a “bullying mentality”.

Mr. Pezeshkian could have talked about reopening the Strait of Hormuz and ending the bombing of the infrastructure, airports, and civilian areas in neighboring countries. He could have attempted to justify why Iran was militarily striking out at these neighboring countries, when Iran’s adversaries were the U.S. and Israel.

What’s vivid in the minds of most people is Iran’s brutal reaction to peaceful protests in Iran. The slogan “Women, Life, Freedom” in 2022, when the so-called morality police arrested and killed a young Iranian student, Mahsa Amini, for incorrectly wearing her hijab (headscarf). Peaceful protests by brave Iranians followed, with the Basij – a paramilitary force under the command of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) – arresting thousands and killing hundreds of peaceful protesters.

Iran can change its behavior and seek to be removed from the State Department list of State Sponsor of Terrorism. That means stop supporting their proxies, the Houthis (Yemen), Hezbollah (Lebanon), Hamas and the Palestinian Islamic Jihad (Gaza), and the Shi’ite Militias in Iraq and Syria, all funded, armed, and trained by the Iran’s IRGC.

But Mr. Pezeshkian did not talk about or attempt to justify Iran’s behavior. He said Iran was the victim.

Russia and China apparently agreed.

In addition to attempting to justify its war in Ukraine, Russia’s Foreign Minister, Sergey Lavros, said Russia was aligned with the Iranian regime, criticizing the U.S. and Israel for its military operations in Iran. Indeed, Russia continues to supply Iran with real-time satellite imagery and tracking data regarding U.S. troops, aircraft, and warships in the Middle East for targeting purposes. Russia reportedly is also providing military hardware to Iran: explosives, ammunitions, drone components, and shoulder-fired man-portable air defense systems.

China’s Vice President, Han Zheng, in addition to touting the impact of China’s Belt and Road initiative, criticized the unilateral military actions of U.S. operations in Iran, while not mentioning anything about Taiwan. And according to the Wall Street Journal, Chinese entities have provided Iran with satellite intelligence, and thousands of dual-use components during the ongoing war with the U.S. and Israel. The satellite imagery reportedly helped Iran improve missile and drone targeting of U.S. bases in the region, to include the U.S. base in Jordan that killed three American service members. Additionally, satellite imagery permits the Iranian military to better track commercial ships and U.S. military escorts in the Strait of Hormuz.

Also of real concern are the reports of dual use shipments to Iran. Reportedly, there were over 1,000 air shipments from China to Iran’s Defense Ministry in the first half of 2026. These included GPS devices, electric motors, aircraft-engine parts and chemical precursors used for ballistic missile propellants.

There are reported plans for China to ship up to 400 Chinese-made shoulder-fired air-defense missile launchers (MANPADS) to help Iran rebuild its defenses. There are also concerns that Chinese front companies and banks helped Iran bypass oil export bans and move billions of dollars through barter and credit arrangements.

Whether China ordered or allowed these reported actions is unclear.

The U.S., supported by Germany, France, and the United Kingdom state that military trade, drone transfers, and ballistic missile exchanges between Russia, China, and Iran are in violation of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2231. Moreover, the U.S. and its allies criticized Russia and China for vetoing a September 2026 U.S – drafted resolution to extend the mandate of on the UNSC’s Panel of Experts on Iran. The veto obstructed lawful oversight of Iran.

It appears that Russia and China are supporting Iran in its war with the U.S. and Israel.

Mr. Pezeshkian portrayed Iran as the victim. It’s the people of Iran and the innocent people killed by Iran-backed terrorists who are the victims.
