item.title: The case for pulling US military back from the first island chain
item.description:
Late last month, Japan’s defense ministry made an unsettling announcement. A U.S. ground-based missile system, known as the Typhon and capable of firing Tomahawk missiles, would not return to the United States after being deployed to Japan for military exercises. Instead, it would be stored at Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, at least temporarily.

Tokyo tried to downplay the move, noting that the decision was intended to support training, not warfighting, and that no U.S. Army units would deploy with the missile system. But the reassuring language is unlikely to forestall the negative consequences of the posture change: an increase in military tensions along the first island chain in East Asia.

The timing of the decision, following closely on the heels of the visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping to Washington, may seem out of sync with Donald Trump’s “dovish” outreach to Beijing. But the contradiction is a feature, not a bug, of the Trump administration’s Asia policy. By calling for a “decent peace” but building a “denial defense along the first island chain,” a region that stretches across Japan, Taiwan, and the Philippines, Trump seems destined to undermine his own efforts to stabilize the U.S.-China relationship and even to increase the medium-term risk of conflict between the two global powers.

The paradox in the Trump administration’s approach to Asia is best articulated in the National Defense Strategy published earlier this year. The strategy lays out two aims. First, it calls on the U.S. military to “set conditions for a balance of power in the Indo-Pacific that allows all of us—the United States, China, and others in the region—to enjoy a decent peace.” Second, it declares the U.S. intention to “erect a strong denial defense along the first island chain to…ensure that the Joint Force always has the ability to conduct devastating strikes and operations against targets anywhere in the world.”

In the Pentagon’s strategic rationale, the latter aim is a prerequisite for the former. This is wrong. Instead, the two goals are fundamentally incompatible. To understand why, it helps to take a closer look at what a denial defense in Asia requires and its practical effects from Beijing’s perspective.

The U.S. interest in building a “denial defense” in East Asia is not new to the Trump administration. In fact, the U.S. military has long used the first island chain as the center of gravity of its military posture in Asia, positioning some 80,000 military forces at bases in Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, and even Taiwan. The primary purpose of these forces is deterring Chinese aggression toward its neighbors (and especially Taiwan) by raising the perceived costs of such aggression for Chinese military planners and political leaders. To that end, the United States has positioned dozens of fighter jets; warships; artillery and longer-range missiles systems; and air defense on U.S. bases along the first island chain.

The Trump administration’s focus has been on strengthening this first island chain denial defense. In addition to the new missile system housed in Japan, Washington is planning to upgrade the fighter jets deployed at bases in the country. It is also building new military infrastructure in Luzon, the island in the Philippines closest to Taiwan, and modifying the types of forces deployed at strategic locations in Japan, the Philippines, and even South Korea. In the future, these personnel will be armed with new anti-ship and anti-aircraft missiles intended to prevent China from projecting military power across the Pacific.

But while Washington describes this military posture as defensive, from the Chinese perspective, the U.S. position along the first island chain is abrasive and threatening. It is not hard to understand why.

Intermediate-range missiles positioned close to the Chinese mainland, fighter jets at bases only a few hundred miles away, and warships patrolling waters off China’s coast can only seem aggressive to China’s leaders. At the very least, such a military presence seems aimed at containing China’s power and interfering with its ambitions in its near abroad—the same types of ambitions that Washington claims in the Western Hemisphere under the “Donroe Doctrine.” At worst, these forces have hostile intent and aim to work against China’s security interests.

It should be unsurprising, then, that as the United States deepens its first island chain investments, China accelerates its military buildup, deploying more missiles on Chinese territory opposite Taiwan and expanding its patrols in the South China Sea and closer to Japan. The net result is not Washington’s “decent peace,” but rather a region that is gripped by an arms race, less secure, and closer to war.

The United States can achieve a decent peace with China, but it will require a willingness to adjust its regional posture, giving up on regional dominance and accepting a balance-of-power approach that creates physical and strategic distance between the U.S. military presence and the Chinese mainland. This balance can be achieved by a shift in the U.S. center of gravity in East Asia, from the first to the second island chain, made up of U.S. territories and the Compact of Free Association states.

Specifically, the United States would reduce and consolidate its military presence, including both personnel and assets, into bases in Guam, Palau, Micronesia, Tinian, and others, leaving at most a small number of rotational forces in Japan and the Philippines. Alongside this change in military footprint, a narrowing of U.S. military commitments would also be required, with expansive mutual defense treaties being replaced by a more sustainable set of narrow security partnerships. There are several reasons why this set of posture changes makes sense.

Most importantly, the outcome of the U.S. war in Iran reveals clearly that the current U.S. first island chain presence is not sustainable or survivable. Defenders of the status quo argue that first island chain bases are essential for dispersing U.S. forces and assets for any contingency situation, such as a war over Taiwan, but bases in Japan and the Philippines cannot serve this purpose if they cannot be effectively defended. Pulling forces back to the second island chain would not make them invulnerable to Chinese attack, but they would be more defensible and significantly reduce the risk of conflict with China.

A second island chain strategy would have other benefits as well. It would be more aligned with core U.S. national security interests, sufficient to protect U.S. access to regional economic markets against physical interdiction and to balance Chinese power in East Asia, especially with the addition of a coherent U.S. economic strategy.

The first island chain denial defense, by contrast, leaves the United States vulnerable to entanglement in unnecessary wars (including one over Taiwan) that the U.S. military today seems unprepared to fight and weakens the incentives of U.S. allies when it comes to investing in their own defense and reaching out diplomatically to China. Finally, the physical space between the U.S. military presence and the Chinese mainland could act to significantly reduce the risk of war between the two countries, creating momentum for the decent peace that Washington says is its ultimate goal.

Critics argue that the opposite is true, that if the United States pulls back to the second island chain Beijing will be emboldened, seizing Taiwan and moving on to assert dominance over Japan and others in the region, before pushing the United States out of Asia entirely. But there is little evidence to support such dire predictions. China, a nation dependent on trade, has little incentive to shut the U.S. out of the region’s economic networks, and it does not have the military capabilities to become the region’s sole hegemon, especially if countries like Japan and South Korea invest in their own military development and work to balance Chinese power.

Of course, U.S. retrenchment would create some new risks, including possible efforts by Japan and South Korea to pursue nuclear capabilities or to over-invest in offensive military capabilities that increase regional insecurity, at least temporarily. But these risks are manageable with a careful U.S. economic and diplomatic strategy. Changes in U.S. posture and commitments can be gradual, for instance, to give countries like Japan time to invest in their own defense and to avoid feelings of abandonment that could trigger a too-rapid build up or race for a nuclear weapon.

The United States might retain security partnerships with current allies that include rotational military deployments and the option for support in a military crisis as well as joint defense industrial projects and economic investment. Finally, the United States should also communicate carefully with China about its planned retrenchment and intention to remain a Pacific power, even while accepting a more narrow remit.

It is true that China would like a smaller U.S. military footprint in Asia, especially close to its shores. But this does not mean that a smaller presence would not also serve U.S. interests. In the longer run, the ultimate responsibility for the region’s stability should not fall on U.S. shoulders but on efforts by the region’s middle powers to achieve a modus vivendi with China that accommodates Beijing’s security interests and makes further military competition unnecessary.

item.title: Can Kurds in Iraq unite as US troops withdraw from the country?
item.description:
On September 21, the Kurdistan Region of Iraq officially announced the completion of the long-delayed unification and reorganization of its Peshmerga paramilitary forces under the Ministry of Peshmerga Affairs (MoPA).

The Peshmerga are Kurdish armed forces, with roots going back to Kurdish guerrillas who fought as a more or less united front against successive Iraqi governments for most of the 20th century. After the 2003 invasion, though, they never came together as one Kurdish national army. Instead, they split into two separate party forces, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) and the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), each tied to one of the region's dominant political factions.

Kurdish leaders hailed the September unification announcement as a historic victory for the Kurds in Iraq. Notably, the unification happened nine days before the final U.S. military withdrawal from Iraq.

The timing raises an important question: as Washington shrinks its direct military presence in Iraq, what security architecture will it leave behind?

A unified Peshmerga could provide a key part of the answer.

From coalition dependence to security partnership


The U.S. has been supporting Peshmerga reform for years, mainly as part of the international coalition's support for the Kurdish fight against ISIS . A memorandum of understanding between the U.S. Department of Defense and the Kurdistan Regional Government in 2022 set out how the U.S. could transform the Peshmerga into a professional military partner.

A newly unified Peshmerga could end up on the front line against Iran-aligned militias and a possible resurgence of ISIS. For the Kurds, this may be part of the logic behind the timing of unification itself: a fragmented Peshmerga would be far less equipped to absorb pressure than a unified one.

There is no clear indication that Washington planned the September 21 announcement as part of its withdrawal strategy. Peshmerga reform has been underway for years. Still, the timing is hard to ignore, and it makes sense to look at the two developments side by side.

For Washington, ending a military mission doesn't mean surrendering its interests in the region, particularly amid a war with Iran. The U.S. interests in Iraq are as follows: first, keeping ISIS from coming back and tempting the U.S. to intervene once more; and second, containing Iran's influence and preventing its spreading into Iraq's state institutions and armed groups, especially with the wider U.S.-Iran standoff still playing out.

Going forward, the plan is for Iraqi and Kurdish institutions to carry more of the load for ensuring security themselves. Meanwhile, the U.S. and its European partners will shift to other kinds of support: training, advising, intelligence sharing, and helping local forces build their own capacity.

The Peshmerga force is situated to help secure U.S. interests, particularly since the Kurdish region’s territory borders Iran. The real question is whether the reform and unification of Peshmerga forces go according to the plan that has been set by the Kurdish leaders under Washington's watch, or the intra Kurdish division prevents the united Kurdish army from materializing.

Can the unification process overcome intra-Kurdish fragmentation?


The real test is whether the new structure that has been outlined by KRG officials changes who commands in reality. Critics highlight that the new Regional Command 1 of the Kurdish Peshmerga forces is led by KDP and that the Regional Command 2 is led by PUK. Also, each command can still appoint their own division and brigade commander.

This suggests that loyalty and allegiance to political parties remains the decisive mechanism through which each command functions. The MoPA did not hide the reality that there is still significant work to be done for the unification to be concluded. In response to the critiques, the Ministry highlighted some achievements that can elaborate on how the KRG can overcome the obstacles of the unification process.

One of the crucial accomplishments of the unification process in recent years is that, nowadays, the payments of the salaries of all Peshmerga forces, regardless of their different commands, have been united through a central ministry account. This means that soldiers’ salaries are tied directly to the ministry, not to political parties.

Kurdish officials say they hope to end party influence throughout the Peshmerga by the end of this year. Prime Minister of the Kurdistan Region, Masrour Barzani says unification is only “the first phase of a long path.”

Whether leaders will truly set rivalries aside is unclear. It has been two years since the region held parliamentary elections, yet it still has not formed a new government. This is due to political deadlock between the two major political parties over sharing the core ministerial and high governmental offices of the KRG.

The question now is whether external pressure can help force the two sides to set aside their differences. Washington has long made unification a condition of providing aid, and its military departure will now increase the incentives for the sides to reach a unified front. As it leaves the country militarily, Washington will have to refocus its diplomatic efforts on encouraging unification in order to help overcome political deadlock.

The Iran factor


If Iran-aligned armed groups refuse to lay down their weapons or turn them over to the state, this presents another issue for the U.S. withdrawal. The duty of disarming the Iranian-backed militias in Iraq — a key step in strengthening the Iraqi state — now falls on the Iraqis.

The American side is leaving Iraq according to a previous agreement with the Iraqi government, which hoped it could disarm Iranian-backed militias ahead of the U.S. withdrawal. However, these groups have resisted calls to give up weapons, saying foreign forces should leave first before disarmament can take place.

At this stage, the groups remain too powerful to easily control, and the Iranian government has a strong interest in supporting them, particularly when they can threaten the U.S.-aligned forces across the region. The coming weeks and months will thus bring a battle of wills between the Iraqi government and the militias it has long sought to control.

What happens now?


The real test starts now that the Coalition has completed its withdrawal.

Iraq appears to be entering a new phase, with fewer foreign troops but continued foreign security partnerships. The Peshmerga's September 21 unification could facilitate this shift, particularly if it overcomes the difficulties inherent to any military unification effort.

What matters now is whether the United States and its European partners can cut back their direct military presence and still leave behind local institutions strong enough to prevent a return of ISIS and keep regional rivals and militia groups in check.

Thus, the U.S. may be leaving Iraq militarily, but the security relationships it spent years building aren't necessarily leaving with it.

item.title: Increase in Hormuz oil traffic is papering over a darker reality
item.description:
Reports that more oil is getting through the Strait of Hormuz have been heralded as a win for the Trump administration, but experts say this kind of happy talk hides the fact that the war remains in a quagmire. As shipping costs rise and Iran continues to attack vessels, world markets — including fuel — will remain in peril for the foreseeable future.

In other words, no matter how much narrative-shaping is attempted to alter American perspectives before the midterms, prices for consumers will not come down to so-called pre-war levels in time for any change. If anything, the diesel crisis continues, as does the impact of ships carrying dry bulk (fertilizer, aluminum, petrochemicals, grains, sulfur, cement, industrial minerals, etc.) still stranded in the Persian Gulf.

Moreover, with news that another U.S. carrier strike group led by the USS Roosevelt has been sent to the Gulf, it is almost certain that President Donald Trump wants to keep the naval presence in place to protect these oil transfers (and perhaps support future military operations). But how long can the U.S. military sustain this costly level of activity in the Gulf in order to keep the fuel markets from going off a cliff? And it’s not like these ships are moving without challenge. Despite what Trump and defense secretary Pete Hegseth say about the obliteration of the Iranian military, attacks on vessels attempting to cross the Strait last week continued, many under the radar of the mainstream press.

So while the administration and its social media influencers have declared victory over Tehran, a very expensive cat-and-mouse game continues unabated — one that Rose Kelanic, director of the Middle East Program at Defense Priorities, says may be impossible to sustain for the long term.

“We're still in this limbo where Iran can't fully close the strait, but the U.S. can't fully open it either,” she tells Responsible Statecraft.

“If the U.S. wants oil to go through the Strait without getting to a peace deal with Iran, it needs to commit a large amount of military force to do that,” Kelanic continued. “Whether that's really sustainable or wise or fair to the American taxpayer is an open question.”

Doing the Persian Gulf limbo


Pro-war influencers like Will Chamberlain took to posting on X “daily reminders” that the “strait was open and we are winning” last week, while blasting "doomers" for saying the war policy has failed and is hurting Americans back home.

What is really happening? There are myriad ways of tracking shipments through the strait: through ships’ Automatic Identification Systems, radar and satellite imagery, and monitoring actual crude volume. Some trackers use a combination of sourcing. Last week, all industry trackers found an increase in ships entering and leaving the strait since the start of the war, with volumes ranging from 13 million to 17 million barrels per day and 6 to 17 tankers per day getting through. This compares to an average of 20 million barrels getting through the strait before the war.

Kpler, a private data and analytics platform, has been the most cited in recent press reports. It said that transits of oil averaged 13 million barrels a day at the end of the month. It is also tracking how much oil is getting out of the Middle East through other ports on the Red Sea on the end of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, which went back on line at the end of September. This bypass route has allowed another 4 million barrels per day to exit the region, according to Kpler.

Much of the higher volume is made possible now by ship-to-ship transfers, notes Amir Handjani, an energy lawyer and public affairs executive, in an interview with RS. This is where private companies come into ports and with AIS transponders off, undergo the very risky and expensive task of transferring fuel cargo into government “shuttle” vessels that travel through the strait “dark” and then offload onto larger tankers in safer, open waters. Ship-to-ship is also used for shuttling through Hormuz bypass routes.

“It’s not moving without cost and without huge investment by the U.S. Navy. Is that sustainable?" asked Handjani. "I don’t know, I guess anything is possible.”

Though government tankers can avoid insurance costs, the premiums on private shipping are increasing, in part because of continued attacks, and supertankers or Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs), which are needed to meet the shuttles on the other end, are now in short supply.

“The paradox here is that physical oil movements are recovering, but the maritime system is doing so through longer voyages, ship-to-ship transfers, rerouting, and extraordinary war risk costs, rather than a return to normal operations,” pointed out maritime expert Sal Mercogliano on the October 3 episode of his podcast. “Add to (that) the ridiculous rates being charged for very large crude carriers — $1.2 million out of the Persian Gulf and $800,000 out of the Gulf of Oman heading to Asia.”

The diesel dilemma 


Any analysis of the situation would not be complete without talking about diesel, which is a refined product of crude. According to experts, the first impact point is the Hormuz chokepoint for oil exports explained above. If and when the crude gets through there are fewer refineries on the other end because of Iranian attacks on Gulf facilities , and refineries in both Ukraine and Russia have been targets in the war there. Moscow has banned exports as a result.

The U.S. is a major exporter of diesel, but it’s not making up for the reduction in global supply. Shrinking supply is wreaking havoc on prices (including in the U.S.), particularly because diesel is used for overland shipping, farming, and transportation throughout the U.S., Europe and the Global South.

Under pressure from the Trump Administration, the G7 countries agreed Friday to release 100 million barrels of crude and diesel from reserves. This is on top of an earlier agreement in March via the International Energy Agency to release 400 million barrels. Trump said the Europeans were not living up to their end and has threatened to ban U.S. exports of diesel, which experts tell RS would be a disaster for prices — in the U.S. and abroad — in the long term.

As for American oil reserves, experts say they are at the lowest point since 1983 thanks to releases of hundreds of millions of barrels by the Biden and Trump administrations during the wars in Ukraine and now Iran. Recent news of vessels getting through the strait won’t make up for all the problems plaguing the system.

“It's all still net negative — the amount that's getting out — compared to what the market demands,” Kelanic pointed out. “We're depleting our inventories more slowly, but those buffers are also much less robust than they were in February.”

Ezana Tedla, a macroeconomic analyst at the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation, tells RS that without a resolution of the war and an end to the threat of attacks on shipping, the markets remain uncertain, which is why Brent crude pricing was still $102 a barrel on Sunday even after all the “good” news last week about the strait.

“By looking at global macro financial data, you can see that there's significant pressure by the unresolved part of the conflict,” Tedla said. He points to a recent research note from J.P. Morgan that basically “said we don’t know what’s going on” and therefore can’t make forecasts about prices, he added.

It is not clear, either, how long the Navy can sustain the tempo to maintain the blockade and the security umbrella needed for ships to pass through, experts noted. The Navy is already stretched thin, with fewer ships to rotate in and out of the Middle East without compromising its security posture elsewhere.

The bottom line is that prices will not come down before voters head to the polls next month. However Trump might spin it, small victories in the Strait of Hormuz do not reflect any end to the war.

“Unless (Trump) signs a deal with Iran of course, that would help a lot,” said Handjani. “That is what the market is really looking for.”

item.title: Russia’s new drive to crush Ukraine
Russias new bombing campaign strangles Ukrainian economy
The world is facing an almighty LNG crunch
The Pentagon’s 2027 Drone Problem
item.description:
On September 30, at Quantico, the Secretary of War announced a four-star command for autonomous warfare. The memorandum behind it is two pages long. It gives two officials 30 days to produce a plan and sets October 1, 2027, as the day the Autonomous Warfare Command stands up. “We do not have a decade,” it says.

On the same day, a California company announced a Pentagon order for 14,000 small attack drones, along with 800 more reallocated from competitors that could not meet their production deadlines. First-round deliveries had been running late, the trade press reported, because the motors, batteries, sensors, and chips that American law will accept were in short supply.

Five weeks ago in these pages I argued that America was buying an army it could not command. The Hegseth memorandum is the most serious answer that argument has received. It settles who buys, and it leaves to the 30-day plan who decides between theaters when the systems run short. It is silent on a prior question. Before a force can be commanded, it has to be built, and this one is being built from parts supplied by the adversary.

The official now charged with building the command has said so to the Senate. “Many of the subcomponents,” Owen West told the Armed Services Committee in March, “do today come from China,” and he put American or allied supply “deep in 2027.” China makes roughly nine of every ten rare-earth magnets in the world. The largest American producer told investors in August that demand for the magnets inside drone motors is met “essentially 100 percent in China.” An American-made drone motor costs $100 to $225; the Chinese equivalent costs $12 to $25. The memorandum asks for a force on “the right side of the cost exchange.” For now, that exchange is priced in Chinese factories.

The trade truce does not reach any of this. Beijing’s ban on dual-use exports to American military users has been in effect since December 2024 and has never been suspended. In June, China added two American magnet makers and a drone manufacturer to its export-control list. The truce itself was extended in September to January 10, yet the notice that suspends China’s rare-earth licensing rules still expires, on paper, on November 10. That is eight days before the President is due in Shenzhen, where he will arrive as the customer for the magnets his own deterrent requires. Beijing does not need an embargo to use this. It needs only to let a notice lapse, and its magnet shipments to the United States had already fallen 21 percent in August.

Washington has set a date of its own. On January 1, the Pentagon’s rule barring Chinese-origin magnets from defense supply chains takes effect. For most of next year, Chinese parts will be barred by both governments while American ones are not yet made in volume. That stretch falls in 2027, the close of the Davidson Window, the year American commanders have named since 2021 as the one by which Beijing wants the option of force against Taiwan. The force meant to deter China in 2027 depends, through 2027, on China’s willingness to keep selling to it.

The picture is not hopeless. Magnet plants in South Carolina, Oklahoma, and Texas are shipping or commissioning, the Army has contracted for millions of magnet segments for drone motors, and in March Ukraine built a drone with no Chinese components at all. The capacity is real. It is also early and expensive, and no one has been given the authority to decide who gets it first.

The money runs through the same gap. In the week the command was ordered, hiring all but stalled, and the 30-year Treasury still ended near its highest yield in 24 years, while France, Germany, and Japan set multi-decade highs. The savers who finance American deficits can now earn more at home. In the same fortnight, Washington threatened to cut anyone servicing Iranian airlines out of the dollar system and warned two allies that American diesel might stop coming. The country is spending the dollar’s leverage abroad while asking the world to finance its rearmament.

That is the economic-warfare lesson inside a defense memorandum. China’s leverage is exercised by a commerce ministry, with a notice, at a time of its choosing. America’s answer is divided among a portfolio office that buys, Services that supply the forces, a Congress that has not written the law or appropriated $53.6 billion of the $54.6 billion requested, and a Treasury borrowing at its highest long-term rates since 2002. Each is competent. As I wrote here last week on the economic front, none is in command.

The plan due around October 30 is the place to change that, and it turns on two decisions. The first is supply. When American-made magnets, motors, and batteries are scarce, as they will be for most of 2027, someone must decide which programs and which theaters receive them, and that decision must bind the Services and suppliers alike. The instrument exists; the priority ratings of the Defense Production Act were written for exactly this.

The second is integration. As this series has argued, the artificial intelligence on which such a force depends must operate at the tactical edge. A drone that cannot compute there and is not connected through a common command-and-control architecture to everything else in the fight is not a capability. It is one more unintegrated system handed to the warfighter, another problem to manage under fire, and one the adversary will render obsolete, because what cannot be integrated cannot adapt.

Supply, integration, and deployment are one problem. Washington has divided it among separate offices, and no one owns the whole. If you have a hand in that plan, see that it names who holds each authority and sets the supply and integration schedules beside the fielding schedule. Otherwise, the command will stand up on time next October with an order book and no arsenal.

Richard Berry is the founder and principal of Stratnova Advisors and a former Commander’s Action Group Director at U.S. Indo-Pacific Command; he publishes the weekly assessment Strategic Horizons.

Hegseth’s Vision for a New American Military
item.description:
“It's worth saying again so that the fake news understands it. We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: No fanny, no fatties, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals, just warriors -- just tough, ready, committed troops. The War Department, as you know, is colorblind, gender neutral, and merit-based. Or, as the President likes to say to me: ‘Pete, central casting. I want central casting.’”

That was Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaking on The State of the Force last Wednesday at the Marine Corps Base, Quantico, Virginia to a group of 600 selected O-3 junior officers (Captains in the Army, Marine Corps, Air Force, and Space Force; Lieutenants in the Navy and Coast Guard) and E-6 enlisted service personnel (Staff Sergeants in the Army and Marine Corps; Petty Officers First Class in the Navy and Coast Guard; Technical Sergeants in the Air Force and Space Force).

President Trump wants a military that looks like “central casting,” and Defense Secretary Hegseth, who looks and acts as if he, himself, came out of central casting, gave last week’s speech, reminiscent to anyone over 45 of the 1970 movie Patton, where George C. Scott playing Gen. George S. Patton also spoke before a full-screen American flag.

“The ideological clowns are out,” Hegseth said, “The patriotic cowboys are in with testosterone testing on top.”

He is correct.

He spoke of bringing back PT (physical training) “for every combat MOS (military occupational specialty),” adding, “We now have a combat field test, again, set at the highest male standard, only because combat doesn't care. That means two PT tests every year for every unit.”

As for picking senior leaders, Hegseth said, “We got rid of the DEI-based (diversity, equity and inclusion), social, emotional, evaluations known in the Army as BCAP [Battalion Commander Assessment Program] and CCAP [Colonels Command Assessment Program]. You won't have to endure them. They were [former-Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Mark A.] Milley and [former Defense Secretary Lloyd] Austin specials, intended to create politically-correct quotas for race and gender. Under the guise of double-blind psychology assessments, the previous administration forced out so-called toxic leaders in favor of promoting risk-averse, get-along to go-along conformists.”

However, Hegseth left out the important fact that BCAP and CCAP were products of the first Trump administration, put together by Casey Wardynski, then-President Trump’s appointed Assistant Secretary of the Army for Manpower and Reserve Affairs.

In prepared testimony for a March 11, 2020, Senate Armed Services Subcommittee on Personnel, Wardynski said, “The Army is currently prototyping, piloting, or implementing talent management initiatives from Talent Based Branching (TBB) to Battalion Commander

Assessment Program (BCAP), with the goal of implementing most of these initiatives by December 2020… Exit interviews and surveys from participants, board members, and distinguished visitors indicate BCAP is better than the legacy system for selecting battalion commanders and other key Lieutenant Colonel positions. Seven hundred and fifty candidates participated in the first iteration of the BCAP in January and February 2020.”

In a September 21, 2020, Army release about testing the new Colonels Command Assessment Program (CCAP) for bias at Fort Knox, Kentucky, Wardynski is quoted saying of the CCAP program, “When we started things like talent management and then this [CCAP], the question of fairness came up. A lot of the focus of fairness was to the individual.”

Although Milley was Army Chief of Staff at the time Wardynski’s BCAP and CCAP were being introduced, then Gen. Austin was head of Central Command and not involved.

Since January 25, 2025, when he became Defense Secretary, Hegseth has changed the senior leadership of the military and even has plans that could affect the leadership in years to come, and I will discuss that below.

First I want to point out that Wardynski was not the only originator that Hegseth ignored during last week’s speech.

For example, former-Defense Secretary Ash Carter and his Deputy Defense Secretary Robert Work in 2015 established the Pentagon’s Defense Innovation Unit (DIU) which was the initial effort to bridge the gap between the Defense Department and commercial technology through rapid investments in autonomous systems, human-machine teaming, and even early Artificial Intelligence (AI).

Project Maven, linked to DIU in 2017, focused on integrating computer vision and AI into drone operations, allowing computer algorithms to autonomously scan hours of aerial drone video footage to detect and tag potential tactical targets.

This sounds a lot like Hegseth’s new Autonomous Warfare Command (AutoWarCom). And to tie the connection further to Carter and Work’s DIU, Hegseth named Owen West, who up-to-now has been DIU’s Director, to be Chief Executive Officer of AutoWarCom.

Then there is Project Meridian, which is supposed to -- in Hegseth’s words -- “Creatively look to the future and identify the domains that we must conquer and capabilities we must master.”

We old-timers knew Andrew (Andy) Marshall and his Office of Net Assessment at the Pentagon which was started in 1973. With a small staff and a wide range of consultants, Marshall covered many areas related to national security. When he retired in 2015, his work was carried on until Hegseth disestablished it in March 2025.

Hegseth’s March 2025 memo called for a plan to rebuild the Marshall office in a manner “consistent with [Hegseth’s] priorities.”

Project Meridian may be that. As Hegseth described it last week, “We need to be looking forward into the future to achieve technological and military dominance on the battlefield for

decades to come. It is futuristic on purpose. Their work will be focused on discovering, developing, and fielding the weapons and systems that our children and our grandchildren will need in their lifetimes without any creative limitations or restrictions.”

Hegseth said last week that he has from the beginning wanted a 20 percent reduction of flag officers “across the board,” adding, “Now, the media calls that a purge. I call it accountability, long overdue and frankly the bare minimum…You see you can't change a culture with the same people who enabled it.”

A list of those fired, compiled by CBS, is impressive: Air Force General Charles Q. Brown, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff; Navy Admiral Lisa Franchetti, chief of naval operations; General James Slife, Air Force vice chief of staff; General Randy George, Army chief of staff; General David Allvin, Air Force chief of staff; Army Lieutenant General Joseph B. Berger III, Army Judge Advocate General; Air Force Lieutenant General Charles Plummer, Air Force Judge Advocate General of the Air Force; Admiral Alvin Holsey, head of U.S. Southern Command; General Christopher Donahue, head of U.S. Army Europe and Africa; Air Force General Timothy Haugh, NSA director and head of U.S. Cyber Command; Lieutenant General Jeffrey Kruse, head of the Defense Intelligence Agency; Air Force Lieutenant General Jennifer Short, senior military assistant to Defense Secretary; Vice Admiral Nancy Lacore, Navy Reserve chief; Rear Admiral Milton Sands, head of Naval Special Warfare Command; General David Hodne, Army Transformation and Training Command; and Major General William Green, head of the Army Chaplain Corps.

In addition, I add Navy Secretary John Phelan and Army Secretary Dan Driscoll.

Needless to say, nothing like this has happened in the past to the U.S. military, and it doesn’t end there. We don’t know the full extent of the individuals Hegseth has knocked off promotion lists, although indications are clear they are most often women and minorities.

In another effort to affect the future, Hegseth not only has sought to force changes in the Service Academies’ curricula and civilian tenured teaching staffs, he announced in last week’s speech an attempt to influence college ROTC units and thus the future generation of young officers.

He also announced establishment of a new program, America’s Core of Cadets, to be initiated at five specified institutions: Louisiana State University (LSU), Liberty University, Tuskegee University, Mississippi State University, and Hillsdale College.

The publication Inside Higher Ed reported last week that LSU will establish a four-year military or national security program; create a self-governed student military organization – a cadet corps -- led by an independent commandant who reports to LSU’s president; and cadet members will be required to wear uniforms during all academic hours.

On top of all this, Hegseth also announced establishment of an Office of Religious Affairs, which will report straight to the Defense Secretary, or as he put it: “No staff filters, no bureaucratic dilution, a direct line to the Secretary. This is not going to be a paper-pushing shop. It's going to have real teeth. They'll protect budgets, demand infrastructure, and strengthen religious support.”

To justify this religious office, Hegseth pointed out, “Less than five percent of our force identifies as non-religious. Less than five percent. Meaning 95 percent of our force recognizes an almighty God.”

As with other statements made by Hegseth, this is not totally true.

According to a 2019 study conducted by the Congressional Research Service, approximately 73 percent of all military service members identify as people of faith, compared to less than three percent who are atheist or agnostic. Religious diversity in the military is broadly representative of the U.S. population, with nearly 70 percent of active duty military personnel who consider themselves to be Christian.

Hegseth said last week, “Our department is, you might say, putting on the full armor of God, because while we wage physical war, we all know the real battle is spiritual.”

Reviewing all Hegseth is doing, as a drafted, two-year Army veteran from the 1950s, I would say our Defense Secretary is taking the spirit of true government service out of the military I have known.

item.title: Despite war US military is leaving a stronger Iraq behind
item.description:
On September 30, the U.S. completed the withdrawal of its troops from Iraq. Heralding this event, Iraq declared “Sovereignty Day,” celebrating the end of U.S. occupation and return of full sovereignty to the people of Iraq.

In practice, this withdrawal was little more than the departure of a few hundred soldiers that had returned to Iraq in 2014 – at the invitation of the Iraqi government – to provide support and assistance to the collapsing Iraqi Army in its fight against ISIS.

Unlike the hundreds of thousands of troops needed in Germany and Japan at the end of WWII, the troops of Operation Inherent Resolve were neither an occupation nor a challenge to sovereign control. Nonetheless, the mission had become a political liability and a convenient excuse for anti-government militias to maintain independence, retain weapons and force its will both in the streets and within Parliament.

While some voices in Washington argue for a keeping residual military presence, the reasonable solution is shifting to a diplomatic and development effort. This was U.S. policy after the first withdrawal in 2011 and should remain the policy going forward. The Strategic Framework Agreement, signed by President George W. Bush and Prime Minister Nouri Al-Maliki in 2008, envisioned this relationship and should remain the policy going forward.

Critics claim Iraq’s security forces aren’t ready to handle their own borders or keep internal order. Senior Iraqi officials, including the national security adviser, have made it clear that premise is wrong. A Higher Military Commission established between U.S. Military leadership and Iraqi counterparts conducted a methodical, benchmarked evaluation to measure the capability of Iraq’s security forces. Today, the Iraqi military is one of the largest conventional forces in the region, certified as sufficiently equipped, organized and capable of managing both internal and external threats.

There is, of course, no guarantee that this preparation would translate into a political will to fight any given enemy. Indeed, the Iraqi military has long suffered from internal political and sectarian divisions. But it is unlikely that the presence of a small U.S. force would make a difference on this front.

A continued American footprint would also have catalyzed continued instability. Illegal, Iranian-backed factions characterize attacks against American troops and shared military facilities as resistance to occupiers, and the retention of major weapons stocks as necessary to fight the Americans. Disarming militias unwilling to answer to the central government is a major policy of Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s administration, but the presence of American troops works contrary to this policy.

It is unlikely a small U.S. presence will deter further Iranian expansion, as some analysts claim. The Iranians have seen serious blows to the strength and influence of their proxies in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and it is likely they will now push harder to keep — and try to expand — their proxy strength in Iraq, regardless of al-Zaidi’s disarmament program.

Additionally, given the current war between the U.S. and Iran, U.S. forces in Iraq would be likely targets of retaliatory Iranian rockets and missiles in the wake of U.S. attacks in Iran. Keeping Iraq and its territories out of the protracted U.S.-Iran war should be a U.S. objective.

The U.S. military departure from Iraq need not mean the end of support to the Iraqi military. Defense cooperation doesn’t require permanent basing or massive combat garrisons. Security assistance, intelligence sharing, counter-terrorism coordination, and specialized training can easily be delivered “over the horizon” or with temporary train and equipping missions, as is done around the world. A security cooperation office – Office of Military Assistance-Iraq – will remain in the U.S. embassy to facilitate these programs.

Ultimately, debating a residual force presence is an academic exercise, not a policy option. The Iraqi government made it clear that it would not renew the 2008 Status of Forces Agreement in 2012, and it is equally unlikely the Iraqi Parliament would do so in 2027. At the same time, neither the U.S. administration nor the American public demonstrates any appetite for another “forever war” in Iraq.

While an existential threat to either Iraq or America might change that dynamic, such a low-probability event should not drive U.S. policy. The U.S. military was invited back to Iraq in 2014 to assist the Iraqi Security Forces in defeating ISIS. That mission expanded when the group’s defeat in Syria was included, but that mission has been accomplished.

Going forward, the relationship with Iraq should be focused on diplomatic and development objectives. The 2008 Strategic Framework Agreement (SFA) set out a comprehensive roadmap for the post-military relationship. That framework prioritized:

  • Economic, financial, and trade cooperation;
  • Energy, diplomacy, and political cooperation;
  • Cultural, educational, and scientific exchanges;
  • Health and environmental cooperation; and
  • Law enforcement and judicial cooperation.

In Iraq, these objectives are as relevant today as they were almost two decades ago. The lead for U.S.-Iraq relations belongs under the pillars of the SFA, not under the auspices of a military mission.

The last quarter century has clearly proven the wisdom of this division of labor. It is best to stop turning to the Pentagon to solve inherently political, economic and diplomatic problems that would best be handled by the Department of State.

How America Wins the AI Race With Open Source
item.description:
Speaking in Shanghai on July 17, Xi Jinping offered the world a vision of AI “for the positive, for good and for humanity.” He called for open source, openness, and sharing. He cautioned against stretching national security to cover the field. And he announced that over the next five years China will train 5,000 people from developing countries, build AI application cooperation centers with ASEAN, the Arab League, the African Union, CELAC, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, and BRICS, and extend its MAZU meteorological warning system to 30 countries. The World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization now exists in Shanghai with 37 member states.

This reasonable sounding offer is aimed squarely at the governments the United States most needs: countries that want AI capacity, local control, and a voice in setting the rules. For these governments sovereignty means control rather than independence, and a system they can operate locally is an easier sell than a remotely controlled API. Beijing pairs capable open weight models and inexpensive inference with training, institutions, and public goods, then wraps the package in the vocabulary of multilateralism and the United Nations.

The results are already visible. CNAS counted sovereign AI initiatives in 67 countries and the European Union by mid-2026, up from 16 governments in 2023, and most model projects with disclosed foundations adapt a foreign open weight model rather than train one. Increasingly that foundation is Chinese. Spain’s Quasar 438B, billed as Europe’s strongest reasoning model, is built on Z.ai’s GLM-5.2. Japan’s Rakuten AI 3.0 uses the DeepSeek-V3 architecture. AI Singapore built its latest regional model on Alibaba’s Qwen rather than Meta’s Llama, and Saudi Arabia’s HUMAIN commissioned its Arabic model from MiniMax. Chinese open-weight models passed the American share of global downloads for the first time in 2025, and on OpenRouter, a marketplace that routes developer traffic to models, their share of usage climbed from under 15 percent to more than half within a year, with businesses in the Global South the heaviest users.

The United States can win this competition, but not just by publishing the most advanced models and declaring victory. It must make American technology the preferred foundation for other countries’ AI systems, as American software and protocols became the foundation of the modern internet. That requires capable models, affordable hardware, financing, training, and dependable support, assembled into an offer that can stand beside a cheaper Chinese full-stack bid.

What America Must Do to Win

Washington should compete throughout hardware, models, software, and services. Retreating to frontier models and advanced chips while China supplies the open models, inexpensive inference, and industrial applications through which most of the world will actually use AI would surrender the contest at the layers where adoption happens.

Openness alone wins nothing. It gives a country seeking local control a reason to consider a model, not a reason to prefer an American one over a Chinese one. The American model must win on performance, total cost, local-language capability, reliable supply, and support, and it must leave room for domestic firms to build businesses around it. Partners deserve honest terms about licenses, updates, and what happens when a supplier relationship ends, and they have reason to ask. When U.S. controls forced Anthropic to suspend access to its newest models from June 12 to June 30, governments learned that even allies can lose access to American systems on a decision made in Washington. Autonomy has to be part of the product, because autonomy is what Beijing is selling.

The model is not hypothetical. An Indian financial firm runs DeepSeek on rented GPUs in India; the weights reside locally, inference never leaves the country, and there is no API for a foreign developer to revoke. Partners want the same from America, with the hardware, financing, and support that make it work. The developers now building on Qwen and DeepSeek show the cost of ceding that ground: expertise accumulates around particular models, models are tuned for particular hardware, and both pull future purchasing with them.

What China Is Doing

Xi’s language of openness should be read alongside that of Chen Yixin, China’s Minister of State Security. Writing in the Cyberspace Administration’s magazine in September, Chen describes AI as a primary battleground of great-power competition. He links political security, espionage, cyber capability, and military transformation to technological independence and control over international governance. An intelligence chief is explaining how AI alters the conditions under which his state exercises power. The two speeches are not in tension. One describes the offer; the other describes the objective.

The institutions Xi announced serve both. A cooperation center with each major regional bloc is a venue where Chinese models, hardware, and standards become the default for an entire region’s developers. A meteorological warning system deployed in 30 countries is a public good that also installs Chinese infrastructure and data flows in 30 capitals; an Egypt-specific version with aviation weather and sandstorm warnings is already in development, while Huawei courts Cairo for its Ascend chips and Malaysia weighs the same hardware. This is the softer sell: adapt the technology to the customer’s existing systems rather than demand reorganization around the supplier, as 01.AI did in building Kazakhstan’s national model. The World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization is a bid to set governance terms in a body Beijing convened, and Xi’s warning against an expansive national security concept is a preemptive argument against the export controls Washington relies on. Washington should engage on international standards, but only where the decision rules leave Beijing no approval power over American development or release, at home or abroad.

Beijing’s openness may not last. Reuters reported in July that Chinese authorities were weighing restrictions on their own frontier models, and the TC260 AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, released September 14 under CAC guidance, points the same way. Alongside provisions on loss of control and autonomous cyberattacks, its treatment of capability diffusion and removable safeguards suggests China may grow more selective about open releases. If so, its position as the default supplier of capable open models may not endure, and the window for an American alternative is open now.

The Tradeoff America Should Accept

Open models cannot be recalled once distributed. That is their appeal to partners, and it means adversaries will use them. The presumption should nonetheless favor open release. Any exception should identify the capability at issue, the security benefit of withholding it, the cost to American adoption, and whether adversaries can obtain comparable capability elsewhere. With a near-peer challenger offering alternatives, withholding American models may merely divert adoption without diminishing adversary capability. Washington can still restrict advanced chip exports for defined security reasons; a partner’s choice of competing hardware is a reason to improve the offer, not to penalize the partner.

Partner autonomy does not require surrendering American authority over domestic release decisions, export licensing, or the integrity of U.S. networks. It requires accepting that American benefits need not depend on a remote veto over systems partners already operate. Government and military users at home should continue to choose systems, closed or open, on performance and security.

What Washington Should Do

The July 2025 AI Action Plan endorses open-source and open-weight AI, and Executive Order 14320 on exporting the American AI stack supplies a framework for coordinated technology packages, diplomacy, and financing. The task is to convert those commitments into an offer that wins.

Fund what the market will undersupply: sustained open releases, smaller-language capability, independent evaluation, and affordable local deployment. Make the complete package competitive, with financing, predictable hardware access, workforce training, and genuine roles for local firms, and resource it as the national security priority it is. The Export-Import Bank’s $66.1 million guarantee for Côte d’Ivoire’s national data center shows the tools exist; it needs to operate at the scale of China’s regional cooperation centers. Demonstrate the bargain with willing partners through a sovereign AI pilot, potentially building on Pax Silica, that discloses remaining dependencies and compares cost, delivery time, and power requirements against the alternatives. Each regional cooperation center Beijing opens should have an American counterpart that partners can judge on results. Then measure the results: which models partners choose, whose hardware serves them, and who earns the integration revenue. A lost American sale does not always deepen dependence on China, and a won one does not always reduce it.

American leadership will prove most durable when partners have their own reasons to sustain it. The test is what countries choose to build, and whether building with America remains worth it to them.

item.title: Russia’s Kaliningrad threats show the value of Baltic preparedness
item.description:
Russia’s Kaliningrad threats show the value of Baltic preparedness Expert comment jon.wallace 7 October 2026

Moscow’s nuclear rhetoric should be taken seriously. But Baltic states know grey zone attacks and territorial incursions are equally serious threats.

Vladimir Putin always chooses his words carefully. If Russia faced a direct attack on Kaliningrad (its enclave on the Baltic Sea), he warned on 1 October, the use of ‘all weapons in (our) country’s arsenal’ would inevitably be on the table. 

The statement followed an earlier Russian note to NATO, threatening nuclear escalation if the alliance were to isolate Kaliningrad. NATO, thus far, has responded with restraint. Secretary General Mark Rutte said there was no imminent Russian threat and rebuffed Moscow’s nuclear rhetoric. But this skirmishing has pushed Kaliningrad – and NATO’s Baltic borders with Russia – back into the spotlight. 

Kaliningrad is not just any territory for the Russians. At the Yalta and Potsdam conferences of 1945, Soviet leader Stalin asserted his claim to what was then known as Königsberg. It was, he said, necessary for Russia to have at least ‘one ice-free port’ at the expense of Germany. The US and UK consented, and Moscow gained a permanent military position on the Baltic Sea. 

After the collapse of the Soviet Union and the withdrawal of the Baltic states to become independent democracies, Kaliningrad’s geographical isolation from Russia became more apparent, creating one of the most peculiar pieces of land on the continent. Today the enclave hosts Russia’s Baltic Fleet, missile systems and combat aircraft. 

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the surrounding geopolitics has changed. Finland and Sweden are now part of NATO. Poland is rearming at unprecedented speed. And the military presence across the alliance’s north-eastern flank is much denser. Meanwhile, Lithuania may soon vote to lift a ban on hosting nuclear weapons on its territory – a move the Kremlin described on 6 October as ‘a step towards escalating tensions’.

Kaliningrad remains a key forward position for Russia. But its near-complete isolation, in the middle of a more coherent NATO Baltic presence, presents Moscow with a serious geostrategic and military challenge.

Denying Russia a quick victory

One glance at the map is enough to understand that Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have but little strategic depth. The three states depend heavily on the Suwałki corridor – a 65km strip of land between Kaliningrad and Belarus that connects Poland and Lithuania – for overland reinforcement. Reclaiming territory from an attacker would be an unlikely option for Baltic countries.

The only credible alternative is to make a Russian advance difficult from the beginning. ‘We have to start from the border and win from the first battles,’ Colonel Tarmo Kundla, commander of the Estonian First Brigade, recently declared.

That is the purpose of the Baltic Defence Line along the eastern border: bunkers, anti-tank obstacles and other defensive outposts. Estonia plans hundreds of squad-level bunkers. A permanently deployed German armoured brigade will become operational in Lithuania in 2027. And Finland now hosts a NATO Forward Land Force. Defence spending across the region has risen far beyond NATO’s old two-per-cent target to reach nearly 5.5 per cent in the case of Estonia.

The intention is clear. Russia must be deterred from any attempt to seize even a small amount of territory – a significant possibility if Russia were to test NATO resolve. 

Preparedness before the first bullet is shot

But Baltic defence measures are about more than spending commitments and defending their Russian borders. Baltics countries know that to deter Russia it is just as vital to stress test their critical infrastructure and train their societies to keep functioning if and when a crisis emerges. Indeed, there is a lot the rest of the continent could learn from Baltic states’ whole-of-society model, which seeks to prepare their entire populations for an era of high-threat risk. 

From Finland to Lithuania, this model consists of embedding all the layers of society in defence and preparedness strategies. This form of ‘comprehensive security’ is grounded in the belief that keeping the country functioning in a crisis is a shared responsibility of government, business, civil society and citizens. In this regard, the Baltics are the most strategically advanced in Europe.

Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania have accelerated preparations for grey zone conflict of the kind in which Russia excels, including attacks on infrastructure. All three have disconnected their electricity systems from Russian and Belarusian networks, progressively synchronizing them with the continental grid since February 2025. In the meantime, NATO has increased protection of Baltic undersea infrastructure, following damaged cables and various incidences of suspected sabotage. 

Slowly learning

Europe’s larger military powers are awaking to the need to somehow follow the Baltic lead and prepare their societies for an enlarging spectrum of threats. Germany, which would serve as one of NATO’s main logistical hubs in any reinforcement of the Baltic region, saw much of its civil-defence architecture fall into disrepair after the fall of the Berlin Wall. 

Its shelter capacity, for instance, now covers only around 480,000 people. Last spring Berlin approved a new €10-billion civil-defence programme, including plans to convert underground car parks, tunnels and stations into emergency shelters – evidence of renewed political engagement.

France has tested its armed forces at scale in the Orion 26 high-intensity exercise, which brought together 12,500 troops, 24 allied nations and civilian institutions in a scenario ranging from hybrid attacks to large-scale conventional war. The UK has developed a 2026 resilience plan that explicitly acknowledges growing Russian sub-threshold attacks. And the government is considering a reserve-style home-defence force to protect critical infrastructure. 

These are important changes. But ‘E3’ countries are still struggling to jointly improve resilience in transport, healthcare, energy, and communications – even as the risk of an enemy trying to disrupt all of them at once grows.

NATO is moving to drive the task forward. Its newly released resilience baseline requirements ask governments to plan for large movements of populations alongside military deployments; to develop health systems that can function even in case of mass casualties; and to develop communications and transport networks that can continue supporting allied forces during high-intensity conflict. In the near future, these will become the pillars on which deterrence actually depends.

Baltic gaps

Still, resilience won’t be enough alone to vanquish an enemy attack on the region. Baltic air and missile defence remains rather thin considering the scale of Russia’s drone and missile arsenal. Reinforcements would still have to reach the region through corridors like the Suwałki gap. And Russia would seize any opportunity to disrupt such movements. Fundamentally, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania remain reliant on their larger allies’ ability to swiftly provide additional forces and air power in the event of a significant attack.

This makes Stalin’s ‘ice-free port’ of Kaliningrad more than an isolated flashpoint on the Baltic shores. Putin’s nuclear rhetoric deserves to be taken seriously. Russia revised its nuclear doctrine in 2024, explicitly broadening the circumstances in which Moscow could consider nuclear use. These include threats to its territorial integrity and attempts to isolate parts of the Russian territory. 

But the military geography surrounding the enclave has changed too. Once referred to as NATO’s most exposed flank, the Baltics have become much harder to intimidate, and harder still to overrun before NATO can respond. 

Related work

Poland could be Europe’s rising star on defence and security

Their experience also carries a wider lesson for Europe: strategic weight is not measured by size alone, even that of a nuclear arsenal. Agility, civil preparedness and political resolve have allowed small states, free and democratic since 1991, to alter the terms of deterrence at their border. 

They have shown Europe that resilience begins long before deterrence fails and that it can change the enemy’s calculation. Their measures will make any attack look potentially far slower and costlier that Moscow would once have believed. Perhaps most significantly after the blatant failure of Russian objectives in Ukraine, Baltic resilience makes overall success of a military attack look far less certain for Vladimir Putin.

item.title: After the RAF Fairford incident, the UK should develop its homeland defence forces
item.description:
After the RAF Fairford incident, the UK should develop its homeland defence forces Expert comment thilton.drupal 7 October 2026

The threat of hybrid attacks from Iran and Russia means the UK should develop a force dedicated to protecting its bases and infrastructure at home. Finland and Poland offer lessons.

The US’s withdrawal of its bombers from RAF Fairford, following a suspected terror plot against the base, has brought attention to how the UK defends its homeland military bases and other critical infrastructure.

The UK government has insisted RAF Fairford is safe following the arrest of five men near the base on 27 September. President Donald Trump said the US withdrew its bombers from the base because of an unspecified ‘threat’ to the base. 

The investigation into the incident is still ongoing. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that there are ‘strong indications that Iran played a part,’ which Iran’s embassy in London has rejected. In March, the UK approved a US request to use RAF Fairford for what it described as defensive strikes on Iran. Tehran responded that any base used for ‘aggression against Iranian territory’ would be a ‘legitimate target’ for its forces.

Bases such as Fairford have their own protection forces that guard the perimeter. But incidents like this highlight the need for the UK to improve its wider homeland defence forces in the face of sustained pressure from hostile actors such as Iran and Russia. 

While the UK has specialist counter-terrorism units that can respond to incidents, and its armed forces and reserves can be deployed domestically to aid civil authorities in a crisis, it lacks a specialist domestic-only force that could protect a wider range of sites for a longer period.

Response versus protection 

The Fairford incident is just one example of the various hybrid threats facing the UK. Alongside Iran, Russia in particular poses a major threat. The Cabinet Office recently announced it would brief the chief executives of UK critical national infrastructure providers and defence firms on the ‘enduring and significant threat’ from Russia. 

Danish intelligence has also warned that Russia could mount a limited military attack against a NATO member within months. Across Europe, states have attributed drone incursions, arson and sabotage to Russia.

Protecting domestic sites is different to identifying the perpetrators or deciding on retaliatory measures. These happen after an attack; protection must be in place before one. This requires forces built for protection, not just response – which is what some UK allies already have. 

Poland and Finland’s approaches

Poland and Finland have both taken a structural approach, creating forces whose primary purpose is the defence of their own territory. 

Established in 2017, Poland’s Territorial Defence Force is the fifth branch of its armed forces. Recruited locally and organized around a brigade in each province, it remains in its own province when Poland mobilizes its forces, rather than reinforcing the regular military. Its stated tasks include protecting critical national infrastructure. 

Related work

Russia’s Kaliningrad threats show the value of Baltic preparedness

Finland’s approach is broader. A permanent security committee coordinates preparedness across government, working from a list of key functions that the state must keep running in a crisis such as water, energy and transport. Military and civilian planning sits within a single framework rather than separate departments. The premise is that defending the home territory is a permanent task, rather than a contingency to be activated during a conflict.  

Neither of these two models directly transfers to the UK. Poland’s territorial force reflects its position bordering Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad. Finland’s rests on conscription and a political culture influenced by its long border with Russia. 

However, the principle beneath both examples is transferable: protecting home territory requires forces raised specifically for the task, not carved out of regular forces each time they are needed. 

The UK has currently not adopted this principle. It does not have a dedicated force assigned to protecting a wide set of UK sites for a long period. 

Architecture without dedicated forces 

The UK is not starting from scratch. 

The Cabinet Office runs the Home Defence Programme, a cross-government effort to align military and civilian planning for threats to the UK. The 2026 Resilience Action Plan implementation report said the programme was being accelerated, with updated crisis response protocols and a planned national home defence exercise in 2027. The Ministry of Defence (MOD) has a Director of Homeland Defence and Strategic Threats. Standing Joint Command is the MOD’s operational headquarters for UK resilience tasks. 

A report published in January by researchers at the University of Exeter set out what this architecture lacks. The report argues that home defence activity is fragmented; that no lead department holds a mandate with executive tasking authority and adequate resources; and that the UK is at a standing start while allies including Finland, Poland and the Baltic states are years ahead. Its recommendation of a designated lead department is a good starting point.

However, even if these recommendations were implemented, a mandate does not produce troops. The UK has a reserve force. But alongside maintaining the UK’s own defence and resilience, this force is also expected to contribute to NATO’s collective defence and can be deployed abroad. 

Relying on the same reservists for both tasks only works while these two demands do not arrive at the same time. UK land forces are designed on the assumption that they will be deployed abroad, rather than defend domestic sites. In a crisis on the European continent, the task of domestic protection would not disappear. It would compete with the demand for British land forces to be deployed elsewhere.

Three changes the UK should make

Three changes follow. The UK should base its approach on the Polish design principle. This means setting up new reserve sub-units with a purely domestic protective role, recruited and based locally. These new units would be positioned near the bases and critical national infrastructure most likely to attract attention, and not counted as reinforcements for deploying formations elsewhere.

The new units would not replace existing forces. Guard forces such as the MOD Police and the Military Provost Guard Service, along with the RAF Regiment for air bases, would remain responsible for perimeters and immediate site security. And specialist units would still respond to incidents. 

Instead, the new units would do what the existing forces are not designed to do: secure non-military critical infrastructure, cover the ground beyond the perimeters, and protect multiple locations during a period of heightened threat. They would be designed to hold these sites for periods of months rather than days. 

This does come at a cost. Every reservist given a home defence role is one fewer available for deployment, and that is a real reduction in what the UK can send abroad. But in a situation when both home defence and overseas demands occur, the choice of home defence will need to be prioritized by default. Making that choice deliberately now means the force is generated and ready before that happens. 

From Finland, the UK should take the treatment of homeland protection as a permanent function rather than a contingency. This means protecting a budget for it, since activity funded from training and readiness budgets is vulnerable when defence budgets are squeezed. The British Army has already reportedly been told to suspend major exercises this year for lack of funds, and in September it was reported that army reservists are set to serve fewer days because of budget cuts. 

Want to hear more on the evolving security landscape?

Join experts and policymakers at our Security and Defence Conference for candid analysis of today’s most pressing threats.

Finally, the UK’s distribution of its protective forces should follow from the government’s decisions and the threats those decisions potentially attract, rather than from isolated incidents. When the government permits an operation from British territory, as it did at Fairford, it should decide the protective requirements at the site and its surrounding areas at the same time. 

The UK has the intelligence capability and the legal framework to protect its domestic sites. It also has the beginnings of a coordinating structure, though it needs a clearer lead. What it now also needs is a dedicated force assigned to protecting those sites across the homeland.
